title: Western Ancestors, Part 2: Katagiri Roshi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett emphasizes the importance of simplicity and presence in Zen practice, encouraging listeners to focus on being a mature and grounded person rather than seeking brilliant insights or great meditative attainment. This approach is rooted in the history of Soto Zen in America, where women like G.U. Kennet Roshi brought this sensibility to North America despite not intending to do so. By embracing simplicity and presence, practitioners can embody Buddha's teachings in the here and now, rather than trying to preserve a precious jewel or attain great spiritual status.

sentences.text: I've been really appreciating lately some of the subtle (or maybe they're obvious, I don't know) aspects of Zen practice.
What we're trying to do is just be real.
Just be mature, just be people.
So we're not gunning for some particular brilliant insight or great meditative attainment.
All the meditation is clearly in the middle of this project of just being a person, a grounded, mature person.
It seems to be a very non-linear process: it goes here, it goes there.
One doesn't really know if one's making progress, but sometimes one sees, reflected in one's friends and loved ones and sangha members, that maybe we're a little less of a nut than we used to be.
And we see it in each other.
So I've just been really appreciating the quality in this style of practice of celebrating the extraordinariness of just being ordinary.
The extraordinariness of just being simple and grounded and real.
We're continuing a project that Talus started a couple of weeks ago, of looking at some of the people who brought this sensibility to North America, to America.
We should say North America, otherwise we're excluding the Canadians and our Mexican friends.
North America.
What about South America?
Anyway, the Americas.

Obviously it's a tricky thing to try to bring over, because it doesn't have a very obvious plan, it doesn't have very obvious guideposts, doesn't have clear steps and stages, and now you're at level three or something like that.
It has a ritual container.
You can bring that over readily enough: you walk this way, you wear these kinds of clothes, you do these ceremonies.
Of course they need to be adapted like crazy to make any sense.
But the essence of it, you can't really talk about directly.
You can only experience, right?

And if you're somebody who was immersed in this way of practicing for 20, 30, 40, 50 years, and you're hanging around with an excited group of young hippies in the middle 60s, how do you go about that?
How do you go about conveying the flavor of that?
I guess you have to be pretty patient.
So two weeks ago Talus spoke about one of these ancestors who brought this sensibility of Soto-Zen to America with great vim and vigor, G.U.
Kennet Roshi, who's actually an English woman.
I forget what her birth name is right now.
And she wasn't even really intending to bring Soto-Zen to America.
She was an English person who trained in Japan very strenuously for five years in the middle to late 60s, and she was actually on her way home to London.
I don't know if Talus mentioned this part, but she stopped in San Francisco because she heard about San Francisco Zen Center.
She wanted to see how they did it, and then she didn't go to London.
She spent the rest of her teaching life in California, which is a classic Zen story.
You're going to do one thing and then 20 years later you're doing something else.
Or maybe it's a classic human story of how frail our imagined plans and intentions actually are.
Anyway, it's amazing the way Talus wove G.U.
Kennet Roshi's story into the story of early Zen women.
So if you weren't here, or even if you were, you should listen to it online.
I didn't realize that Keizan, our famous second Zen ancestor from 13th into 14th century Japan, had a grandmother who was an early supporter of Dogen and a colleague of Dogen.
Eihei Dogen, our first founder, born 1200, died 1252.
Talus cleverly, he posted this online, noticed that there was an alternate lineage through Keizan's grandmother and mother down to Keizan, in addition to the traditional lineage.
Because that's what I'm realizing about this quality of Zen, about how it's centrally about just being a mature, grounded person.
That's why I'm just thinking today, the lineage is put in the middle of all this.
It's not like the myth, like we might have thought, that the lineage chart, these famous diagrams that show a teacher to student, a teacher to student, and then go back to Buddha.
It's not that there's some precious thing that Buddha had that got handed down.
Like this jewel.
And now I'm, I think, the 94th generation after Buddha, so now I've got this jewel and I'm going to hand it to the next person.
No, it's more of a direct horizontal link: when we're really inhabiting this lineage, we're just being Buddha.
No big deal.
Just being Buddha.
Just being that real.
So anyway, of course the male lineage misses quite a bit of this possibility of the linearity and the horizontal nature of all this.
One little additional wrinkle in that story that's interesting is the Rinzai Zen teacher that Dogen and Keizan's grandmother Miochi studied with, named Myozen.
He actually went to China with Dogen.
He went to China with Dogen.
And in China, Myozen got sick and died.
So I was thinking about how isolated and alone young Dogen must have felt.
He was 24 years old in a foreign country in a strenuous training monastery.
That's what he wanted.
He was probably psyched too, but he was probably also overwhelmed, right?
He doesn't write about that in his writings, how freaked out he must have been.
And although he, like other educated Japanese people of that era, knew a lot about China, and he knew a lot of Chinese, they don't pronounce it like the Chinese people do.
So he wouldn't have been able to have conversations with people.
He doesn't mention that either, but that's very clear, scholars tell me.
Maybe they communicated in notes.
Or sketching out characters in their hands.
And Japanese, by the way, is full of so many homonyms that people in ordinary conversation sketch out which character they mean by that sound, which might have 20 or 30 characters associated with it.
So anyway, there he is, and the teacher he came with dies.
Crazy.
So that's one little wrinkle in that story.
And it's wonderful the way Thales pointed out that all the Buddhism and Zen are, for the most part, reflections of the sexist cultures that they emerged in.
Here we have in both Dogen, Heihei Dogen and Keizan Jyoken, the founders of Japanese Soto Zen, strong support for the training of women.
Dogen, in his famous collection of essays, Shobogenzo, has a whole essay about this that we should study sometime.
In Keizan, as Thales was saying, he was constantly listening to his grandmother and his mother.
Once his grandmother died, she kept talking to him in his dreams, which he took very seriously.

So I thought I'd add a few more notes about what Jiyu Kennett Roshi was like when she was first setting up shop in America, and a little reflection from one of her first students, a lovely man that I've met a few times named James Ford.
It's interesting, the many paths.
James is both a Zen teacher and a Unitarian Universalist minister.
He'd actually just retired from that position.
He was a minister of a large congregation in Providence, Rhode Island.
And he's a great writer.
I have here a kind of memoir called *If You're Lucky, Your Heart Will Break*, which is a great teaching all by itself, the title: *If You're Lucky, Your Heart Will Break.*
He talks a little bit about his story and then weaves in quite a bit of Zen thought and Zen history.
Here he's talking about his first work with Kennett Roshi.
She actually wasn't around all that much for him, really.
So a little reflection about one of Kennett Roshi's serious students is kind of a mirror of how Kennett Roshi taught.
James writes:
*A few years after I started sitting regularly,* this is like '68 or '69, *I decided I wanted to be a priest.
I figured if only I were ordained, then all my problems would be solved.* Zen would solve my problems, which is how they thought.
*The difficulty was that the San Francisco Zen Center expected people to go through a very long apprenticeship, which could take many years, and that didn't make any sense to me.
Besides, just getting to speak to the master seemed beyond me.
I attended Suzuki Roshi's talks, but he was always a very small figure, very far away, speaking in what my friends assured me was English, but to my ear was nearly incomprehensible.

I was brooding over this barrier to getting everything fixed when another Zen master, Jiyu Kennett, accompanied by two senior Western disciples, an American and a South African,* who both ordained with her in Japan, by the way, *arrived in San Francisco.
She was English, had studied in Japan for a number of years, and was the Dharma successor to a very prominent Japanese Soto Zen master.*

*Kennett Roshi had been authorized to start a Zen center in London, and on her way here from Japan, stopped over at San Francisco Zen Center to learn how they had successfully adapted Zen training to Western culture.
She hadn't been there a week before she decided it would be better to just hang out her shingle in California, rather than head back home to England.
She moved into a flat on Potrero Hill and announced that she was receiving visitors, and I was the first person at her door.*
*I began sitting at her zendo housed in a little flat, and quickly and formally became her student.
It was exhilarating.
We sat a lot.
I met in private interviews with her daily.

She gave small, intimate classes on various aspects of the Dharma, beginning to guide me and the rest of her small band of students to a larger insight into the Zen way, particularly focusing on the insights of both Eihei Dogen, the founding master of Japanese Soto Zen, and Keizan Jokin, who reformed Japanese Soto into the largest Zen school in Japan.*
*Most important to me was that in one of my first interviews with her, she told me to stop counting my breath and to practice Shikantaza, to just sit.
She didn't elaborate a lot.
She liked the phrase silent illumination, a term probably associated with the master Hongzhi in the early 12th century.
It didn't help very much.* Hongzhi is 11th century, actually.
*It didn't help very much.
I found my mind was neither silent nor illuminated.
Silent illumination.
Not silent, not illuminated.*
*But I persisted.
After I had had a few intensive months with her, the Roshi decided* [unclear: "she had returned"] *to England to wind up family affairs.
Both of her parents had died since she left the country.
She invited me to move into the temple and cover the rent while she was in England and left the South African disciple in charge of the Sangha and took off for London.* So this is the disciple.
*Myozen Delport, the disciple left in charge, was an Afrikaner who had left her home to study karate in Japan.
She settled in and was very successful in her studies and at the same time became deeply involved in Zen practice.
Among her friends was a young man who became infatuated with her.
Focused on her karate and particularly on her Zen practice, she didn't really notice him and didn't really notice his growing feelings for her.
One day she had a long conversation with him where she spoke about her desire to ordain and expressed no desire in him.
And the next morning she learned that he had hung himself.
Haunted, Myozen sought to throw herself completely into Zen practice.
She obtained her introduction to Kennett Roshi, who told me how she'd sat her new student down in the tiny Zendo and had her meditate day in and day out.*

*Every once in a while the Roshi would come in and violently strike the young woman across her shoulders with the Kyosaku, the encouraging stick made for this purpose of startling, punishing or encouraging people in the meditation hall, depending.* Depending [unclear: "on the pronunciation of the stick"], depending on the pronunciation of the word, the stick was said to awaken or to warn.
*In this case it was to drive her forward.* That's kind of how they practiced, they were intense.
*And it did.
The ghost haunting her quickly moved on to easier pickings while Myozen learned how to help someone just sit in a serious way.
When I wasn't working, I was sitting.
Every morning, every evening, most of every weekend.
And periodically Myozen would come into the small Zendo with her Kyosaku and strike me on the shoulders.*
It drove me forward.
It drove me inward.
It focused everything.
Now one doesn't need the stick, I'm moderately confident.
But for me, it pushed things along a bit faster than otherwise might have been the case.
But really, the deal is pretty simple.
All one needs is to just sit down, shut up, and pay attention.
This is the universal solvent of the heart.
Become as wide as the sky.
Let the whole of what is play across the screen of the mind and heart.
Just notice.
That gives a little flavor of Ken Hiroshi's style, and the general style in those days.
And I read a little bit of Ken Hiroshi's autobiography too.
I don't know if you looked at that, but it's amazing.
It's incredibly detailed.
She writes at length about getting herself admitted to the all-male Soto Zen training monastery, Sojiji, which was indeed founded by Keizan.
But the original one was on the other side of the country.
But anyway, her strong will is what comes through.
I didn't read the whole thing.
It's like 800 pages long.
It's like a dozen pages, but it's all the same, pretty much.
It's all about her incredible integrity and stubbornness and personal power, and her refusal to do anything she didn't want to do.
There are several passages about how the Japanese wanted to make use of her as a media figure, to show off that they were liberal and enlightened and letting a woman train there.
And she would just refuse.
They'd show up with their camera crews and stuff like that, and she wouldn't come out of her room.
She wasn't there for that.
And there's another thing I ran into in there where she had one Japanese priest who was her advocate, but he wasn't very high up in the hierarchy.
So he would coach her on how to lie to the higher-up [unclear: "habits"] to get admitted, how to flatter him and how to say the right stuff.
And she would refuse to do that too.
She said, "I'd rather you throw me out now than make me be anything other than completely have full integrity."
So she was an incredible person, and you can gather from this what she might have been like to study under.
You know what I mean?
But very amazing.
She got through five years of formal Japanese training and a hell of a lot of hazing.
Went through the whole system.
Received Dharma transmission.
Started her own monastery in California.
Started her own order.
Came up with her own style of practice, completely from scratch, with her students helping.
So, an amazing person.
I was thinking about how all of religious history, maybe all of history, tends to have golden ages.
The golden age of Zen in China, when all the Zen stories are set and all the Zen koans are set, was the Tang dynasty, which is about from year 700 to 960.
But it was actually the Tang dynasty as it was described by the Zen people in the next dynasty.
It was during the Sun dynasty that Dogen went to China.
So it's kind of funny.
I thought of this one time about five or ten years in.
I said to Norman, "Did nothing happen after year 960?
That's worth writing down.
Why is it all just this one group of characters?"
And he was like, "We studied Dogen too, a little later.
But a lot of things must have happened between now and back then."
It's kind of beautiful having a golden age, because it gives you a consistent universe to talk about.
And these stories are symbolic, right?
They're not exactly what really happened.
But then I was thinking about this talk, that in American Zen we also had a golden age.
We also had a golden age, which is kind of what we're studying now.
We're studying the golden age of American Zen.
Our golden age more or less got started at the end of the 50s, when some Americans started going to Japan, Gary Snyder amongst his friends.
But it really started in earnest in the middle 60s.
Maybe we should date it to 1966, when San Francisco Zen Center purchased Tassajara and started the first Zen monastery in the western hemisphere.
And at the exact same time, Zen centers were forming in Los Angeles, New York, Hawaii.
Kenneth Roshi, whom we were just talking about, started her order in 1969 and her monastery in 1972.
Stuff was happening.
Stuff was really happening.
There were big donations showing up.
Big properties were being purchased.
I guess things were cheaper then.
I can't imagine how they did all this.
And there were populations of utterly full-time, 24-7 Zen students, like James was describing, working and sitting and working and sitting in a very intensive, insular kind of way.
And the golden age, let's say, continued until about 1984.
We'll use San Francisco Zen Center.

So we'll start it in 1966 with Zen Center's purchase of Tassajara, and then we can end it in 1984, when Richard Baker Roshi left San Francisco Zen Center in disgrace, after a terrible series of abuses of power and sexual misconduct.
And sadly, soon after that, the transgressions of other important Zen teachers
became coming to light, and the golden age sort of collapsed in a blaze of chaos.
I was reading about the origins of the idea of the golden age, which comes from Greek mythology.
There are different ages: bronze age, golden age, lots of ages, and each one has different deities involved in it.
It was Cronos who was in charge during the golden age, it turns out.
Anyway, the point historians make about golden ages is that golden ages are always created after the fact.
Golden ages never actually happen while they're happening.
They only happen before.
That's the only time they can happen: in the past.
So golden ages are fun, but they're important.
They're helpful.
They help us organize our understanding, even though we know that they're kind of made up.
I arrived at San Francisco Zen Center in 1987, soon after the collapse of the golden age and the dawning of the pedestrian age of American Zen.
I was raised up there on stories of how hard they worked, how hard they'd practice, and how deeply they really believed in trying to penetrate right to the very bottom of this way.
And how powerfully they idealized their teachers.
So the golden age was a time of great teachers.
If you were a teacher in the golden age, you were a luminous great teacher.
I think that's partly because it was a very small number of teachers, and they were mostly from Asia.
So there were some cultural things happening there, some orientalism or reverse orientalism.

But I think a lot of it was that these teachers became great because they were amplified by their students, and amplified by the headiness of the times, and how new and cool and utterly counter-cultural all this was.
That's hard for us to remember now, I think.
If you were in Zen, you were really sticking it to the man.
You were stepping outside of the entire thing.
Even the way of thinking and formulating thoughts and concepts, you were just leaving all that behind.
You weren't just not participating, you weren't even in the same university.
It's as radical as you can get.
And I think the power of that in the 60s is probably hard for us to understand now.
Maybe some of our elders here remember it better than I can, since I was born in Generation X myself.

And then the other piece was that they had this incredible, motivating, powerful, literal belief that sooner or later there was going to be, without question, a mind-blowing enlightenment experience that was going to change everything.
We just have to sit harder and work harder and revere the teacher more.
So nowadays Buddhism is not counter-cultural anymore.
The Dalai Lama is like a rock star who fills stadiums.
We all love Thich Nhat Hanh, and the reporters on 60 Minutes are studying mindfulness.
We still do believe in awakening, but we don't have quite the same attitude about it.
Not just a single mind-blowing experience.

The process of practice and awakening can have its dramatic moments and its surprises and its insights, for some of us more dramatic than others, but overall we see it as a more gradual settling into our innate maturity and opening to our deepest self that's been right there all along.
And teachers are important to us still in the pedestrian age, or the bronze age, but they're not important to us like gods anymore.
The teacher plays a critical role in the training mandala, but there are lots of other things that are equally important.
One piece, and probably mandala is a good expression.

So it's interesting that all this has happened, and that we can look back these next couple months at the golden age of American Zen and see who these key teachers were and what they were teaching, and see what we can learn from them.
Anyway, after Suzuki Roshi arrived in San Francisco in 1959, he was not there to start a Zen center.
There was no such thing as a Zen center then.
The idea had not been thought of yet.
He was there for work.

He was there to be a parish priest, essentially, and take care of the Japanese congregation in San Francisco, first and second generation and some third generation young Japanese wanting to go to the temple.
But pretty soon he started receiving the attention, as you know, of hippies interested in meditation.
And pretty soon he needed some help teaching these scruffy guys about Zen.
Especially some years later, the congregation gave him an ultimatum.
They basically said, "You know what, it's us or them.
We thought you were here to take care of us and to do the rituals and teach us, and what's with all these guys?"
At the time, Suzuki Roshi, I think without a whole lot of skill, probably didn't consult the board of directors or make a plan or anything like that.
He was just inviting them into the temple and having zazen meetings, and they would hang around, you know what I mean?
They would hang around a lot.
So anyway, pretty soon Suzuki Roshi needed some help.

How could he bring this full package, the full container, the full feeling and spirit of Zen training to these young people, young men and women in America who were so focused on this as one intense aspect of it?
Well, a few years later, in 1963, another Japanese Soto priest, a man 24 years younger than Suzuki Roshi named Dainin Katagiri, was also sent to America by the Japanese Soto Zen Church.
Some of his superiors wanted to send him to Brazil, actually, where there's a larger need, many more Japanese immigrants in Brazil, and even still there's quite a large Soto Zen community in Brazil.
But he managed to arrange to go to America because that's what he wanted.
He was interested in English and all things American.
So they sent him to Los Angeles.
But for reasons that are not clear, that job didn't work out.
He didn't like working with the Japanese congregation in Los Angeles, and he actually quit his job.
Which I think must have been kind of weird at the time.
Got him into America and he's like, "Thanks a lot, this isn't working for me."
Doesn't seem like a very Japanese thing to do.
But he really wanted to stay in America, and somehow he got fixated on the idea that he should go to college in San Francisco.
And he actually did not know about Suzuki Roshi.
Well, it turned out, unlike most of his contemporaries, Katagiri wasn't born into a temple family.
His family, although they were devoutly Buddhist, it was in a different school of Buddhism, the Pure Land School.
And so as a boy he grew up doing daily services at home with his family, and a priest would come like once a month to do special ceremonies.
Turns out in Pure Land they're less temple centered.
It's more home centered.
Everything happens around the home and altar.
There are temples, but they're less important.
And then, like many of us, Katagiri got more seriously interested in what Buddhism really means to him through tragedy.
At the age of 14 his mother died, and the next year the war started.
And I didn't know this, but all boys in Japan 13 years and older were required to join the military or work in weapons factories, to be a part of the war effort.
Young Katagiri for some reason wanted to be a pilot.
Maybe it was a kind of escape from all this, but he flunked the pilot exam or something, and he ended up a mechanic.
But he's still a boy right now, 14 or 15.
He ended up servicing planes, and he also ended up servicing the planes of the kamikaze pilots at the air base where he was.
During the war he lost track of his father.
Communications were bad, and imagine how chaotic this would have been, right?
Imagine yourself at 15.
Your mother's died.
You've lost track of your father.
But eventually, after the war, he returned home.
His father had been a kind of hapless businessman, trying one thing that didn't work out and then another.
Eventually a restaurant business had worked out.
But when Katagiri finally got home, he discovered that his house and his father's restaurant had burned to the ground.
His father only lived a few more years.
So Katagiri Roshi was sort of thrust into adulthood early, still supporting himself as a mechanic and still a teenager, maybe just about to turn 20.
He said something later about this time:
*The situation in Japan was very confused.
Not much food.
Lots of problems over housing.
Transportation was not good.
Jumping on trains, people screamed and pushed into windows.
And there was fighting and even killing each other.
So I could really feel how transient and fragile human life was.
I started to have some doubt about working in the company.
Carrying a pencil in a lunch box.
Building diesel engines.
Could I really spend my whole life like this?
One day I went to my high school friend's Shin Buddhist temple.
It was very peaceful there.
And I had the same feeling I had in the monastery before and after the war.
I was very impressed by monastic life because somehow it had not changed even through the war.
Everything else had changed.
But monastic Buddhist life had not changed.
Everyday routine.
Zazen, chanting sutras, morning services, afternoon services.
Everything was exactly the same.
And the atmosphere was tranquil and peaceful.
I was very impressed.
I decided that was the answer.*
I'm a little like James Ford.
That will solve my problems.
So he ended up being a Zen monk.
And the story goes that it was mostly because that was who was handy to ordain with.
It wasn't really a very active choice.
Not so sectarian.
Now we fast forward to 1963.
Katagiri recounts that he didn't know about Suzuki Roshi, but he had this focus on San Francisco as a place to find himself.
These are Katagiri's words again:
*I wanted to go to college in San Francisco to make some money by myself and study English.
I already had a [unclear: "schoolboy's"] place to live.
But I was caught by Jean Ross, one of Suzuki Roshi's American students.
I had helped her when she visited Japan and she remembered me and wanted me to help at the Zen Center.
She said, "Please don't live separately from Zen Center.
Please help us."
But I was not agreed.
"Just go see Suzuki Roshi."
So finally I went to Sokoji Temple and saw Suzuki Roshi.
He immediately said, "Oh, what a good opportunity.
Please help us."
Even though I decided I wanted to go one way, here was a completely different way.
So I was completely caught by Suzuki Roshi.
Then I met the students of the Zen Center and they said, "Please come.
Please help us."
I was completely caught by everybody and finally I couldn't say no.
So I decided to come to Sokoji anyway.*
But Katagiri didn't really want to just be Suzuki Roshi's assistant.
He didn't want to be a worker bee for the Soto Zen Church, or a worker bee for the diesel factory.
Eventually, through various connections, he found his way to Minnesota, where there was a cluster of interested American Zen students but no teachers.
He said later that he'd heard that all the few teachers there were would just skip the middle of this huge country.
They would just go to San Francisco or New York and skip everything in between.
So he wanted to go where no one else was going to go.
That was kind of his personality.
*I wanted to go where I was really needed and where nobody else would go.*
It's hard to say whether it was more about being needed, or more about no other Japanese Zen priest bothering him if he went to Minnesota.
He did continue helping out at San Francisco.
When Suzuki Roshi died, he stayed a year longer than he wanted.
But then he did go and start a center in Minnesota, the Minnesota Zen Meditation Center.
I think another reason he couldn't stay at San Francisco Zen Center is that Richard Baker was such a big presence.
There was no room for any other teacher.
Richard Baker was the teacher.
Then after Richard Baker flamed out, Katagiri came back and helped out some more.
But mostly he wanted to establish his own practice place and help the people in Minnesota.
But after Richard Baker left and San Francisco Zen Center was in crisis, he would come.
He was a temporary [unclear: "avid"].
He would come periodically to lead training periods and lead sesshin.
That's where I met him, in the fall of 1987.
He might have been the first Japanese Zen priest I ever met.
I was probably as susceptible to the romanticization of the Japanese Zen priest as anyone else.
But still, in a deep way, I was impressed by his presence.
He was a pretty small guy, stalky but very small.
There was just such gravity to him.
I think I learned how to [unclear: "duke in him"] by watching him.
Each step was just solid.
When he took a step, he took a step.
His English was pretty wonky.
Just like James Ford trying to listen to Suzuki Roshi, he had a lot of trouble following the Dharma talks.
I remember two phrases he used a lot.
He would say, "Just do it.
Just do it.
Blah blah blah blah.
You're thinking this, you're thinking that.
Just do it."
Then he would say, especially during Zazen, *Settle the self on the self and let the heart flower bloom.* Have you heard me say that before?
This later expression, it turns out, Blanche Hartman, a wonderful Zen ancestor of ours, took up and has kept alive for a long time.
I remember he was really kind to me when I went to Dokusan, the private interview.
It was my first Zazen and I was trying so hard.
I don't know why I didn't burst a blood vessel in my head, I was just so intense.
I was in so much pain.
Finally, around the fifth or sixth day, something shifted and I had some kind of release.
It was a whoosh of relief.
Suddenly joy and delight had some room to flood in.
I wasn't blocking it anymore.
I remember when I was invited to go see Katagiri Roshi in Dokusan.
I said a little of what had happened, and I had no idea how much I should say or if he even understood what I was saying.
Then he said something like, "Whoa, maybe some small enlightenment.
Very nice."
I was [unclear: "too odd"] to ask any questions.
I was like, what does that mean?
I don't know about enlightenment exactly in my case, more like a release of insane amounts of pressure.
And actually, lots of stress and pressure does contribute to big experiences in meditation.
So if you want to have [unclear: "a blow at awakening"], you know what to do now: just get really stressed out for a long time.
But of course there's more to it than that.
When things release and clarify, sometimes there is some big experience or some big shift.
Other times it's much quieter.
I think it's partly just karmic, and where we all wire differently.
Some of us will never have a dramatic experience in meditation, and it doesn't mean it's not working.
I worked with somebody for a while whose problem was that she got so many darn visions that they were distracting, and she wanted to figure out how to stop them.
Really vivid, hallucinating visions.
People are different.
Anyway, from the mid-70s until his death, Katagiri, like Suzuki Roshi, also died young, also from cancer.
He died in 1990.
He focused on developing the Minnesota Zen Meditation Center and also a rural place that he hoped to make into a training monastery called Hokoji.

In the last few years of his life, and this I didn't know until I was just reading this, he put all of his energy into very carefully completing the training and Dharma transmission of the 14 priests that he ordained.
This is a big deal, actually.
